subject: Plotting in Trajectory Analysis - means in wrong location?

messages.author: 088e8a47a714e2a7
messages.subject: Plotting in Trajectory Analysis - means in wrong location?
parts:
I am performing a trajectory.analysis on data containing two species at four ontogenetic stages. The landmarks were superimposed via GPA in a previous step and formatted as a 2D array using two.d.array and then combined with the classification variables in a dataframe called HPF. Here is the code I am using:

TA<-trajectory.analysis(shape~species*ds, iter=999, data=HPF)
summary(TA)
TA$aov.table
plot(TA, group.cols=c("magenta", "blue"))

Here is the resulting plot:

The centroids of each group seem to be offset toward the negative end of the first PC. Does anyone have any idea why the data is plotting this way and how I can correct it?

Thanks, 

Karen

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Plotting in Trajectory Analysis - means in wrong location?
parts:
Karen,

What is the issue you believe is occurring?  The overall mean appears to be 0,0, as it should be.  The first PC of fitted values tends to separate species, which one would expect if species are clearly different in shape.  What do you mean by off-setting to the negative end?  The centroid for Trog is clearly positive for PC1 score

I’m not sure how you are trying to interpret this but I can clearly see species differences in shape and much more shape change for Trog compared to Homo during ontogeny, although the direction of shape change seems somewhat consistent.  Does that differ from the test you performed?

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Plotting in Trajectory Analysis - means in wrong location?
parts:
I see.  Here are some possible explanations:

  • It is possible that this results from PCA performed on the fitted values rather than the observed values.  When performing PCA in SAS, did you simply perform PCA on the data or did you use the fitted values to generate a covariance matrix before projection of the original data?
  • It could be projection distortion because of huge shape difference between species.  The offsetting seems largest in the most distal group of Trog.  This seems less likely though.
  • It could be a functional error that is only now being revealed with your extreme example.  I have looked at the code and I do not think this is a direct problem, but I see how it could look like one, which brings me to the next one
  • Data imbalance.  The PCA is performed on the trajectory points (fitted values, yes, but not weighted fitted values).  Although there has to be balance among trajectory points, your example shows that you have more Homo specimens than Trog specimens, correct?  Therefore, the center of gravity for trajectory points can be shifted away from the center of gravity for the entire sample.

I think the fourth case is most likely and would not have been revealed earlier if most people tend to have close to balanced data.  If you were to perform PCA first and then take the means (centroids) of PC scores, this would not happen.

I am going to see if I can update the code and ask you to try your analysis again, after I update it (by installing from Github).  If it works, then I will be more convinced that accounting for imbalance is important.

I’ll have the updates done in a couple of hours.

Mike

Hi Mike,

I've made trajectory.analysis plots that look like Karen's before. I assumed it related to projection of observations, but did not bother to follow up. It will be great to see how this gets resolved. 

Your most recent response also seems to answer another question I have had about trajectory analysis, but I want to be sure I'm understanding you correctly. The 2013 Hystrix paper says the PCA is performed on the "covariance matrix of group means." Applying that to Karen's data, I've always wondered if that would mean species means, or species-stage means. I think you've basically answered that question above: "the PCA is performed on the trajectory points," i.e., the species-stage means. Is that right? Moreover, if the function call includes two models (f1 and f2), which set of factors (those in f1 or f2) define the group partitioning for PCA?

Thanks very much!

David

parts:
David,

The “means” are the trajectory points, define both by groups and sequence factors.  While our statement from the 2013 Hystix paper is not incorrect, taken in its most literal form - as the function currently does - weighting is ignored.  For example, the fitted values from a factorial ANOVA are the means for the different factor combinations; i.e., the trajectory points.  In a matrix of fitted values, some means will be represented more if one group is over-represented compared to another.  The pooled-covariance should be a weighted average, perhaps; i.e., the covariance matrix should be calculated from all fitted values rather than just the means.  For balanced data, this produces the same covariance matrices.

Mike

Karen,

What you did seems to be the same thing the trajectory,analysis function does except that you were centering the combined matrix (the trajectory.analysis centers each separately).  What looks appropriate though is probably a partial solution, as each centroid has equal weight.  So, you pulled residuals (observations - mean of observations plus group means) toward the group means.  The observations and their means will line up better, but you do not stay honest to the center of gravity of the scatter in the plot being the same as center of gravity of the data sample.

I suspect that generating a covariance matrix from the fitted values of the model, shape ~ species * ds, which will be different than the covariance matrix of means if one species is over-represented, will appropriate shift the means to align with the mean-centered data, as both would have the same overall mean.  Stated another way, the mean of your centroids is not the same as the mean of your data if the data are imbalanced, but the mean of the fitted values (which has means equal in number to group sizes) is the same.

For balanced data these considerations are not needed.  For nearly balanced data, imperfections are probably unnoticeable.  For substantially imbalanced data, apparently, we have learned projections will not be accurate.

Please be aware that not of this discussion impacts the trajectory analysis, just its visualization.

Mike

parts:
Dear Everyone,

As a conclusion to the issue discussed in this thread, let me report here the important points.

1. This was a plotting issue, not an analytical one.  Trajectory analysis involves finding the LS means for groups and sequential points in many permutations to define trajectories.  This was not in dispute.
2. Visualizing trajectories means projecting these means onto principal components.  Before projection, the means must be “centered” so that the overall mean is 0,0,0,… and covariance matrices calculated from these values are appropriate.
3. Centering by the mean of the LS means - the default when calling prcomp in R scripts - only works if sample size is the same for each group.  
4. If group sizes are different, then means need to be centered by the overall mean of fitted values, which equals the overall mean of the data, rather than the mean calculated from the input values in prcomp.

We performed 3, not 4, in geomorph, but trajectory.analysis has been updated on Github to use appropriately weighted LS means.  You can install the update with,

devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”, ref = “Stable”)

For those of you who have deeper R skills, you might be aware that the prcomp function has a “center” argument.  Leaving this NULL means the function calculates the mean from the data input.  That was the projection problem we had (did not center the LS means by the correct center of gravity), which goes undetected if data are balanced, like in our trajectory,analysis examples.

Many thanks to Karen for bringing this to our attention and helping to beta-test the updates!

Cheers!
Mike

What seems 'off' is that the trajectories themselves (which just connect neighboring ontogenetic stages) are each offset from the clouds of points for their respective species. In other words, I'd expect the trajectories to be more-or-less centered within the distribution for each species, but they are not. When I generate a comparable plot elsewhere (in SAS), the centroids for each stage and the resulting low-dimensional projections of the trajectories are centered within the respective distributions.

I think this is perhaps related to centering that is done for the plotting? But that's just my guess.

I hope this is clearer...

Thanks, Karen
